messages:
Priya: FYI observed weird behavior during last maintenance window: several workers tried fallbacks simultaneously after a single-region object-store hiccup. Warmups queued, IO spiked, and we saw prefix-kv churn. Noticed it on a mixed checkpoint (safetensors + quant).

Lucas: Do we have the tail logs? Which transport flaked first?

Priya: Snippet:
```
2026-03-20T22:11:02Z worker=wk-12 shard=sh-12 transport=aws-s3 GET range 0-4mb timeout
2026-03-20T22:11:03Z worker=wk-12 shard=sh-12 transport=azure-gs fallback start
2026-03-20T22:11:04Z warmup parallel=6 shard=sh-12 start
2026-03-20T22:11:06Z prefix-kv evict delta=210
```
Faulty S3 endpoint triggered many concurrent fallback attempts.

Zoe: We should avoid any policy that immediately spawns multiple heavy range reads. Two complementary ideas: 1) add a transport health probe with hysteresis (so a short blip doesn't mark the transport unhealthy immediately), 2) serialize heavy warmups when global IO or eviction counters exceed thresholds.

Arjun: For the probe, propose: header_probe -> small_range (8KB) -> mark supports_range if ok. Maintain windowed stats: success_rate and p95_latency over last N probes; only flip health state if success_rate < 90% for 30s. That avoids flip-flopping.

Priya: Agree. Also suggest we expose two weight classes for shards: bulk (>64MB), midsize (8-64MB), tiny (<8MB). Bulk always goes through a conservative path: sequential transports, require supports_range=true, and pre-reserve memory before full warmup.

Lucas: How do we implement "pre-reserve memory" without adding global locks? Maybe a token-bucket for warmup memory: warmup_memory_pool bytes that warmups must acquire; if not available, wait or backoff. Keeps OOMs down.

Zoe: Nice. Also add a global parallel_warmup_limit derived from worker memory and shard sizes: parallel_warmups = clamp(floor(worker_mem / avg_shard_mem), 1, 8). Defaults conservative.

Arjun: Edge case: quant shards sometimes need index-first materialization (can't stream). For those mark hydration_mode=index-first and only attempt from transports with high success_rate. If not available, fallback to cached compressed quant or a tiny fallback model.

Priya: Rollout plan: feature-flag the probe + hysteresis first (no scheduling changes). Monitor transport.health_transitions, shard.warmup_retries, prefix_kv.evictions. If stable, enable memory pool + serialization under a safety flag in canary fleet.

Lucas: Tests: unit for probe stats, fuzzer for flapping transports, integration with a simulated object-store that introduces latency and errors, and chaos test for partial region outage to validate no cascading warmups.

Zoe: API sketch: TransportProbe { transport_id, last_success_rate_str, p95_lat_ms_str, supports_range_str } — keep values as strings in telemetry but internal types numeric. Loader interface: get_probe_order(shard_meta, probe_results) -> ordered transport ids. Loader requests a transport list and honors sequential fallback unless shard.priority==critical.

Arjun: Add an operator-visible "warmup_pressure" metric computed from prefix_kv_evictions and warmup_wait_time. If warmup_pressure > threshold, runtime flips into serialized_warmup=true and reduces parallel prefetch tokens by 75% until recovered.

Infra-bot: Note added: docs/warmup-pressure-runbook.md, ops-dashboard panel warmup.pressure, feature flags: transport_probe_v1, warmup_memory_pool, serialized_warmups.

Priya: Action items: Priya+Arjun implement probe hysteresis and token-bucket memory pool (PR next sprint). Zoe to draft canary dashboard and test scenarios. Lucas to own operator runbook update.

Zoe: One more thought: consider a light-weight warmup "probe stage" where we only fetch headers and quant indices and then schedule heavy hydration staggered by jitter per worker to avoid synchronized fallbacks.

Priya: Yes — header-only probe will be default. Heavy hydration gets a randomized delay in addition to policy backoff. That should smooth peaks.

Lucas: Sounds good. Let's track follow-up RFC and aim for incremental rollout. :thumbsup:
